Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP This Is Europe World news ‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German city where the far right surged After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes next Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Kate Connolly in Magdeburg Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Asking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist” , that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly. Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said. Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air. A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s post-war memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”. I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past. Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums. And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.” Fragrance of power View image in fullscreen A damaged banner depicting the top candidate of the far-right AfD party, Ulrich Siegmund, the day after the elections in Magdeburg. Photograph: Annegret Hilse/Reuters It remains unclear how precisely the AfD, led by charismatic former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, might take the reins of power in Saxony-Anhalt, if at all. He lacks an absolute majority by a whisker. There have been rumblings for days – even prior to the election – of an AfD charm offensive to try to lure members of chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, to make up the necessary numbers. The CDU denies any defections are expected. Some AfD members have brazenly appropriated Ronald Reagan’s appeal to the Soviets to “tear down this wall”, from his 1987 speech in West Berlin. They are calling on mainstream parties to “tear down the firewall”, a reference to the Brandmauer , or refusal to ever coalesce with the AfD in an effort to prevent the far-right populists from coming to power. Yet an increasing number doubt that the firewall will hold much longer. Especially now that almost one in two of those who cast their votes on Sunday have opted for the party. Turnout at 78% was a record for the state. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Whatever the outcome, we can expect weeks, even months of wrangling. Expect stasis in the meantime on the federal government front, as we’re close to elections on 20 September in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, where the AfD is also expected to do well. Merz will be wary of doing anything that might drive more voters away. At the same time politicos in Berlin are debating how long he has in the job. In the Bundestag today, Merz accused the AfD of seeking “ethnic cleansing”. No wonder Maryam, 16, whom I met as she returned from work experience at a retirement home, said she and her family were on edge. The Syrian teenager, whose father arrived in Germany in 2015, followed by her and her mother, told me she couldn’t stop thinking about what this vote might mean for her family. She wished, she said, for a return to the days of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor who welcomed in a million migrants including Maryam’s father, resentment over which turbo-charged support for the then-fledgling AfD. Across the road, Doreen, a cleaner, who reluctantly admitted voting for the AfD, said: “What on Earth is there to thank Merkel for? It’s owing to her that we are in the state we’re in.” She recalled an attack near the Christmas market in the city centre in 2024, where six people were killed when a Saudi doctor drove a car into the crowd, an incident that helped fuel support for the AfD. “That attack is symbolic for a whole lot of misery, the decision to open our doors to strangers has brought us,” Doreen told me. “I say, good on the AfD for promising to clean up the mess.” For such a small state, home to 2.1 million people, Saxony-Anhalt has managed to create a political maelstrom, the ramifications of which will be felt across Europe . https://local12.com/news/local/east-pric.text: CINCINNATI (WKRC) — Residents in Cincinnati’s Price Hill neighborhood are taking to the streets to push back against violence, trash, and illegal activity in an area they say has been plagued by problems for years. The hope is to make it harder for violence to take root. "There's definitely crime in the area. We try to do our best to keep it away from this part, but we can only do so much," said Steffani Pruitt, a Price Hill resident. The Price Hill Safety Community Action Team, also known as Price Hill Safety CAT, organized a “safety walk” centered around Olden Tot Lot. It's an area long-time volunteer Patti Hogan says has had its issues. "It's drug activity, drug dealing, and prostitution," said Hogan. Hogan said the event is a precursor to a more in-depth project aimed at drilling down on problems in the area and developing solutions and responses. "We're going to clean up litter, and we're going to have some people sitting in the park to socialize," said Hogan. While Hogan and others went to surrounding areas, officers with the Cincinnati Police Department and volunteers, like Marvin Dickman, helped pick up trash inside the park. "I hope that we can keep East Price Hill a cleaner, safer, and greener community," said Dickman. Hogan said a shooting happened in the area in July and said the recent killing of 14-year-old Rakeem Blair Junior—who was shot and killed about half a mile away—has added urgency to the effort. "We're making a statement tonight; we're reclaiming this park in this area for valid public use," said Hogan. Local 12 asked Hogan what she would say to those who may believe this effort is for naught. "I tell people sometimes I feel like we play whack-a-mole, we'll spend time here, and then in five years, we could be right back. I'm not going to tell you that hasn't happened, because it has," said Hogan. "Starting today, we're punching back." The Price Hill Safety CAT is working on a new community problem-oriented policing (CPOP) project in the vicinity of Warsaw and Woodlawn Avenues. That includes Olden Tot Lot, where the safety walk took place Wednesday night. They plan to hold meetings in the near future to discuss problems in the area and begin to formalize their response to those issues.
